summary:
Public Law 118-185, the "Swanson and Hugh Butler Reservoirs Land Conveyances Act," directs the Secretary of the Interior, acting through the Commissioner of Reclamation, to convey all right, title, and interest of the United States in specified Federal land at Swanson Reservoir and Hugh Butler Reservoir to Hitchcock County and Frontier County, Nebraska. 

Section 3(a)(1) requires the Secretary to make good faith efforts to negotiate and enter into title transfer agreements with the respective counties not later than 3 years after enactment. Conveyances must be in whole, without subdivision, and include a plan demonstrating the counties' technical and financial capability to operate and maintain the land permanently, and to comply with applicable State fire, safety, and health codes within 2 years after conveyance. Section 3(a)(2) provides that, notwithstanding 43 U.S.C. 2902(3)(B), negotiations must adhere to subtitle A of title VIII of the John D. Dingell, Jr. Conservation, Management, and Recreation Act (43 U.S.C. 2901 et seq.).

Under Section 3(a)(4), consideration for the conveyance is the fair market value, determined by a Secretary-approved third-party appraisal conducted under the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice. Appraisals must exclude permit-holder improvements, account for future U.S. revenue streams, and resolve disputes per 43 C.F.R. 2201.4. Payments are available to the Secretary, subject to further appropriation, for reservoir operation activities. Counties must pay all survey and administrative costs in advance. Section 3(a)(5) requires the counties to manage the conveyed land for substantially the same purposes as of enactment, or for recreation and public purposes under the Recreation and Public Purposes Act (43 U.S.C. 869 et seq.), public access, fish and wildlife habitat, or natural character preservation.

Section 3(b) prohibits subsequent reconveyance except at no cost to recognized Nebraska public or governmental entities, provided an adverse impact is demonstrated, the entity has management capacity, and public access continues. 

Section 4 makes conveyances subject to valid existing rights, operational requirements of the Pick-Sloan Missouri River Basin Program (Flood Control Act of 1944), flowage easements, mineral rights, existing permits, deed restrictions prohibiting new permanent structures below specified elevations, and access easements. The United States disclaims liability for flood damage or permit-holder acts, and counties must indemnify and hold the United States harmless. U.S. liability remains capped by the Federal Tort Claims Act (28 U.S.C. ch. 171), and temporary flooding is expressly not a taking. 

Section 5 provides that existing management agreements and permits remain in effect during the interim period ending 3 years after enactment or upon conveyance. If no agreement is executed within 3 years, the Secretary must manage the un-conveyed land in accordance with applicable law.
